notes:
Below are notes on Genesis 27:24–46, verse by verse, with the page URL after each point. I ran out of searches before I could reach some of the sites on your list. I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, the Lutheran or Pentecostal sites, or any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses, so those areas are left blank or only partly covered. Most of the older commentators came through StudyLight or BibleHub pages that collect several commentaries on one page.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 24:** Guzik says Jacob held to his lie even when questioned again. He partly took advantage of his father's good nature, because Isaac probably would not believe that his Jacob would lie to him so repeatedly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
A Ligonier devotional says Jacob's protest earlier (vv. 11–12) shows he was worried that he might get caught, not that he might dishonor Isaac. It also says his life afterwards shows God disapproved of how he got the blessing. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jacob-deceives-isaac

**vv. 25–26:** Bible.org (Utley) stresses that the meal was the setting for handing on leadership of the family. In Hebrew thinking, once the spoken blessing was given it could not be taken back (cf. vv. 33–38). https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-27
Matthew Henry suggests Isaac asked for this meal as a mark of respect. Since marrying, Esau may have been taking his game to his wives rather than his father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_027.cfm

**v. 27:** Henry says the smell was like the sweetest flowers and spices. It appeared that God had blessed him, and therefore Isaac would bless him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_027.cfm
Calvin says he is not unhappy with Ambrose's allegory: Jacob, the younger, is blessed while dressed as the elder, and the borrowed clothes give off a scent his father enjoys. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom02/cache/calcom02.html3

**v. 28:** Barnes reads this as a promise of fertile land. Plenty of dew mattered especially in a country where rain falls only in two seasons, and "grain and new wine" stand for every other product. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/genesis/27-39.html
Guzik notes that the images of plenty echo God's covenant with Abraham (Gen 12:1–3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/

**v. 29:** Guzik says Isaac's words did not make Jacob blessed. Jacob was blessed because God chose him before the twins were born (Gen 25:23). What counted was God saying the older would serve the younger, not Isaac saying "be master over your brothers." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
Utley thinks "may your mother's sons bow down to you" reads almost like a deliberate put-down aimed at Jacob, since Isaac believed he was talking to Esau. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-27

**v. 30:** Guzik points to the dramatic timing: Esau came in almost as soon as Jacob left the tent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
Calvin says the way Esau was turned away helped confirm Jacob's blessing. Isaac declares that what he did in his office as patriarch has to stand. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom02/cache/calcom02.html3

**vv. 31–32:** Guzik pictures Esau hunting and cooking happily, sure of the blessing and the wealth that came with it. He probably took "Who are you?" for an old man's simple mistake. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/

**v. 33:** Several commentators note that the Hebrew is very strong, roughly "trembled with a very great trembling." Sources: Calvin https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02.v.i.html, Utley https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-27, Guzik https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
Utley and Guzik both say Isaac finally saw that he had been fighting against God's plan (Gen 25:23), not that he was simply angry with Jacob. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-27 and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
Calvin says there is no doubt that his fear springs from faith. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02.v.i.html
Guzik links "he will be blessed" to Hebrews 11:20 ("by faith Isaac blessed…"). He quotes Spurgeon's point that Isaac never thought of taking the blessing back, because he sensed God's hand in it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/
Adam Clarke says Isaac would have reversed the blessing if he could. Because it had been given in a solemn, almost "sacramental" way, he could not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-33.html

**v. 34:** Calvin says Esau's cry shows despair. He gets nothing from it because he enters not by the gate of faith. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02.v.i.html
Chuck Smith says these were not tears of repentance but bitter tears over losing the blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-30.html

**v. 35:** Utley calls Isaac's statement a "half truth." I only saw a fragment of this comment and could not read his full reasoning. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-27

**v. 36:** Guzik says Esau cannot honestly claim Jacob "took" his birthright. Esau gave it away, and God is Lord over the birthright anyway. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Gen/Gen_27.cfm
Henry agrees. Instead of repenting of his own folly, Esau unfairly blamed his brother for a birthright he had sold fairly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_027.cfm
Haydock (Catholic) says Esau's ungodly and cruel ways made him unworthy. Having given up his claim under oath, he could not now insist on it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/genesis-27.html

**v. 37:** Calvin finds Esau's request odd. Only one blessing had been entrusted to his father, yet Esau asks for another, as if it were in his father's power indiscriminately to breathe out blessings, independently of the command of God. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02.v.i.html

**v. 38:** Calvin is harsh: Esau ignores his soul and turns to satisfying his body. If he wanted his own good he should have accepted a place under his brother. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/calcom02/cache/calcom02.html3
Guzik is gentler. This is the most spiritual concern Esau has shown so far, though it is still mixed with material and political worries. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Gen/Gen_27.cfm

**vv. 39–40:** Ligonier calls this an "anti-blessing." Edom, south of the Dead Sea, is drier than Canaan, which fits the words "away from" the richness and the dew. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lesser-benediction
Henry notes that nothing in Esau's blessing points to Christ or brings Esau into God's covenant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_027.cfm
Gill and Henry both see the breaking of the yoke fulfilled when Edom rebelled and set up its own king in Jehoram's day (2 Kings 8:20). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/genesis/27-40.html
Barnes traces the history: Saul and David defeated Edom, and in 129 BC John Hyrcanus forced the Edomites to be circumcised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-37.html
Constable says Esau's descendants would live by hunting people, as Esau had lived by hunting game. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-37.html

**v. 41:** Spurgeon mocks the idea that Esau was a sincere penitent, pointing to his plan to kill Jacob. That, he says, is not the repentance that comes from God the Holy Spirit. https://archive.spurgeon.org/sermons/0239.php
One commentary quoted on BibleHub says Esau went the way of Cain, wanting to stop Jacob's line from ruling by killing him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-45.htm

**v. 42:** Keil and Delitzsch say the Hebrew for "consoling himself" means getting comfort by taking revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-45.htm
Henry says Esau's rage was too violent to keep hidden, and that is how his mother found out. https://studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-45.html

**vv. 43–44:** Matthew Poole notes that Rebekah's "few days" became twenty years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-44.htm
Gill adds that Rebekah may never have seen Jacob again. She is not mentioned after this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-44.htm

**v. 45:** Most explain "lose both of you" by blood-revenge. If Esau killed Jacob, the nearest relative would have to kill Esau (Gen 9:6). Sources: Clarke https://studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-45.html, Keil and Delitzsch https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-45.htm
Calvin thinks the mild Jacob would never fight back. Rebekah expected God himself to avenge the murder. https://studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-45.html
The Cambridge Bible suggests "both" might instead mean Isaac and Jacob, since Esau planned to kill Jacob on the day of Isaac's death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-45.htm

**v. 46:** Clarke and Calvin both say Rebekah used a real complaint to hide the real reason. Calvin thinks she did it to spare her husband a mortal blow and to avoid inflaming Esau further. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-46.html
Gill says Esau's wives troubled her with their idolatry and bad temper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-46.html

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**Was Jacob's lie excusable? (v. 24; the whole scene)**
- **Methodist (Wesley):** On v. 46 he calls Rebekah's words "more artifice still," adding that once we use guile we are ready to use it again. He speaks plainly of Jacob's vile lying and dissimulation, which brought him years of suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/genesis-27.html
- **Reformed:** The Geneva Bible notes say Jacob had the blessing by faith but did wrong to seek it by lies, worse because he misused God's name. Poole says the lie cannot be excused, though God graciously forgave it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-19.htm
- **Calvary Chapel (Guzik):** Jacob cared only about what worked, and used God's promise as an excuse for sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/

**Esau's tears and Hebrews 12:17 (vv. 34, 38)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Hypocrites weep like Esau while their hearts stay shut. Esau was destitute of faith and repentance, so it is no wonder he was rejected. Ligonier repeats this. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02.v.i.html ; https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/isaac-and-esau
- **Baptist:** Spurgeon reads this through election. He holds to "Esau have I hated" exactly as written and says God's mercy never followed Esau. https://archive.spurgeon.org/sermons/0239.php
- **Methodist (Clarke):** Clarke reads "no place for repentance" as no change of mind in Isaac, because the blessing had already been formally granted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-33.html
- **Baptist (MacLaren):** What Esau sought with tears was the blessing, not repentance. He did truly change his mind, but it could not undo the past. MacLaren rejects the idea that a person can long to repent and be unable to, calling that a slander on God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/hebrews/esaus-vain-tears.cfm

**Was Esau's blessing good or bad? (v. 39)**
This is a real translation question.
- **Methodist (Benson):** Follows the older "of the fatness" reading and calls Mount Seir fertile, watered by dew and showers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/genesis-27.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Also reads it as a real but lesser blessing. God gives good land and weather even to those outside his covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/27-37.html
- **Reading "away from":** Gill and Trapp mention Castalio's "away from / without fatness" reading and Edom's desert country. Ligonier and Guzik (citing Barnhouse) also read it this way. Barnes notes that the same Hebrew preposition appears in Jacob's blessing. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/genesis/27-39.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/genesis-27.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-27/

---

## 3. Other views

**Catholic and early church (vv. 24–33):**
- In *City of God*, Augustine calls Jacob's trick a profound mystery of the truth rather than fraud. The goatskins picture one bearing others' sins, and the blessing is a proclamation of Christ to all nations. In his reading, Isaac's trembling comes when "the great mystery" is revealed, and he confirms the blessing instead of complaining. https://biblehub.com/library/augustine/city_of_god/chapter_37_of_the_things_mystically.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) reports that Augustine's *Against Lying* clears Jacob of lying. Challoner allows that if it was a lie at all, it was only a small, well-meant one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/genesis-27.html
- The Pulpit Commentary, a Protestant work, calls these defences laborious excuses. It also mentions Theodoret's and Aquinas's argument that Jacob had bought Esau's place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-19.htm

**Jewish interpretation (v. 40):** Benson quotes the Jerusalem Targum: Esau would break the yoke whenever Jacob's sons neglected the law. Benson thinks this fits David's conquest and the later revolt under Jehoram. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/genesis-27.html

**Modern scholarship (v. 46):** The Cambridge Bible (via BibleHub) treats v. 46 as part of a different source ("P") from the main story ("J"). In that source, Jacob is sent away to find a wife, with no mention of the deception. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/27-46.htm
